title: The Use of Context in Assessment
author: 100% Assessment
summary: This article applies Karl Maton's Legitimation Code Theory -- specifically his concept of semantic gravity -- to assessment design, arguing that the choice of context in an assessment question is not neutral but determines what cognitive move students must perform and which students are structurally advantaged. Semantic gravity describes the degree to which knowledge is tied to a specific context (high) or abstracted from context (low). A contextualised question (force applied to a shopping trolley) requires students to perform context-stripping before applying abstract knowledge -- an additional cognitive move that is itself a teachable skill, not a natural advantage. The article introduces 'semantic waves' -- the pedagogically productive oscillation between abstract principles and concrete examples. Good teaching rides semantic waves deliberately: moving from concept to context and back. Assessment designers should understand which position on the semantic gravity spectrum their tasks occupy and what cognitive move they are actually testing. The practical implication is that teachers should explicitly teach context-stripping as a skill. Students who have been taught to recognise the abstract principle hiding inside a contextualised question perform significantly better on contextualised assessments than students who encounter them cold.
points: Semantic gravity measures how tightly knowledge is bound to a specific context: contextualised assessment questions require students to strip the context before applying abstract knowledge -- a skill that must be taught, not assumed.

The familiarity of a context in an assessment question is not a measure of accessibility: students who recognise the context have one fewer unfamiliar variable to manage, regardless of their mastery of the underlying concept -- an equity concern.

Semantic waves -- deliberate movement between abstract principle and concrete example -- should be mirrored in assessment design, with teachers being explicit about what position on the spectrum their questions occupy.

Context-stripping is a teachable skill; students who receive explicit instruction in it significantly outperform peers who have only encountered abstract questions when facing contextualised assessments.

Assessment designers who do not consciously position their tasks on the semantic gravity spectrum risk testing context-familiarity rather than conceptual understanding -- a validity problem with equity implications.
quotes: When we talk about context in assessment, we often assume that more context means more accessible. Karl Maton's work invites us to question that assumption. A contextualised question does not remove cognitive demand -- it relocates it.

Semantic gravity is high when knowledge is tied strongly to its context of application; it is low when knowledge is abstract and context-independent. Neither end of the spectrum is inherently harder, but they demand different cognitive moves from students.

The semantic wave is the pedagogical gold standard: moving students from the abstract to the concrete and back again, repeatedly, until the journey in both directions is fluent. Assessment that stays at one extreme tests only half the wave.

When an examiner writes a question about a shopping trolley in a supermarket car park, they are not making physics more friendly. They are requiring students to perform an act of context-stripping: to look past the trolley and see the force diagram hiding behind it. That is a skill. It should be taught.

The equity problem with contextualised assessment is not that disadvantaged students are less intelligent. It is that unfamiliar contexts impose a dual cognitive load: process the context and retrieve the concept simultaneously.

Good curriculum design rides semantic waves deliberately. The concept is introduced abstractly, embodied in a context, stripped back to the abstract again, then embedded in a new context. By the third or fourth wave, students can move fluently in both directions -- and that fluency is what contextualised assessment is actually measuring.
